canonical_facts.publication: Published 19 October 1847 as 'Jane Eyre: An Autobiography' under pen name Currer Bell by Smith, Elder & Co.
canonical_facts.helen_burns_death: Helen Burns dies of consumption (tuberculosis) in Chapter 9 — NOT typhus. A typhus epidemic does sweep Lowood and kills other students, but Helen's death is a separate event from a pre-existing condition. Jane creeps to Miss Temple's room, finds Helen, falls asleep beside her, and Helen dies with Jane's arms around her neck.
canonical_facts.bronte_sisters_cowan_bridge: Charlotte's sisters Maria and Elizabeth fell ill at Cowan Bridge (Clergy Daughters' School). They were REMOVED from the school and died at home in Haworth in May and June 1825 respectively, of tuberculosis. The school's poor conditions contributed to their deaths; they did not die at the school.
canonical_facts.typhus_vs_consumption: Typhus and consumption (tuberculosis) are completely different diseases. Typhus is a louse-borne bacterial infection; consumption/TB is a mycobacterial respiratory disease. Confusing them or defining one as the other is factually wrong.
canonical_facts.rochester_injuries: Rochester loses his LEFT hand (crushed, amputated by Mr Carter the surgeon) and sight in both eyes in the Thornfield fire. Two years after marrying Jane he regains partial sight in ONE eye, enough to see their first son.
canonical_facts.bertha_location: Bertha Mason is confined to the third floor (third storey) of Thornfield — technically not an 'attic', though that term is common. Bertha jumps from the roof/battlements, not specifically the attic.
canonical_facts.bertha_origin: Bertha Antoinetta Mason — daughter of Jonas Mason, West India planter, of Spanish Town, Jamaica. Her mother was Creole. Rochester married her 15 years before the novel's present.
canonical_facts.celine_varens: Céline Varens is a French opera DANCER (not 'opera singer'). She abandoned Adèle and ran away to Italy with 'a musician or singer'.
canonical_facts.adele_age: Adèle Varens is just under ten years old when Jane arrives at Thornfield.
canonical_facts.inheritance_split: Jane inherits £20,000 from Uncle John Eyre (Madeira). She divides it equally 4 ways: £5,000 each to Jane, St John, Diana, and Mary Rivers.
canonical_facts.proposal_setting: Rochester proposes to Jane in Chapter 23, Midsummer Eve, in the orchard garden under the horse-chestnut tree. Lightning splits the tree that same night.
canonical_facts.interrupted_wedding: Chapter 26. Solicitor Mr Briggs presents written evidence; Richard Mason (Bertha's brother) corroborates in person. Rochester married 'Bertha Antoinetta Mason' 15 years before. Rochester does not deny the marriage.
canonical_facts.mason_attack: Chapter 20. Bertha stabs and bites Richard Mason on the third floor. Jane tends Mason's wounds at Rochester's request; Rochester forbids them to speak to each other.

key_quotes.reader_i_married_him: Chapter 38. Jane is the grammatical subject — she married him.
key_quotes.i_am_no_bird: Chapter 23, proposal scene: 'I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will.'
key_quotes.poor_obscure_plain_little: Chapter 23: 'Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?'
key_quotes.i_care_for_myself: Chapter 27: 'I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself.'
key_quotes.women_feel: Chapter 12: 'Women are supposed to be very calm generally: but women feel just as men feel.'
key_quotes.laws_and_principles: Chapter 27: 'Laws and principles are not for the times when there is no temptation.'
key_quotes.clothed_hyena: Chapter 26: 'the clothed hyena rose up, and stood tall on its hind-feet.' Rochester about Bertha.
key_quotes.caged_eagle: Chapter 37: 'The caged eagle, whose gold-ringed eyes cruelty has extinguished.' Jane describing Rochester at Ferndean.
key_quotes.bigamy_ugly_word: Chapter 26: Rochester: 'Bigamy is an ugly word!'
key_quotes.NOT_jane_eyre: 'I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun' is Mr Darcy's line from Austen's Pride and Prejudice Ch 60 — it does NOT appear in Jane Eyre.
key_quotes.mad_cat: 'Like a mad cat' is applied to JANE at Gateshead (Ch 2) — not to Bertha Mason. The dehumanising animal imagery used for Bertha is 'clothed hyena' (Ch 26).

canonical_facts.st_john_rivers: St John Rivers is Jane's cousin, a clergyman at Morton. Plans missionary work in India. Proposes to Jane for utility (Chapter 34) not love. Loves Rosamond Oliver but suppresses his feelings. Name pronounced 'Sinjin'.
canonical_facts.mrs_fairfax: Housekeeper at Thornfield — distantly related to Rochester but NOT a close relative. Jane initially mistakes her for the owner.
canonical_facts.grace_poole: Servant employed to keep Bertha Mason confined. When Grace drinks, Bertha escapes and causes havoc. Used as a red herring by Rochester to explain strange events.
canonical_facts.veil_scene: Chapter 25 (night before the wedding). Bertha enters Jane's room, puts on the wedding veil, looks in the mirror, then tears it in two. Rochester later confirms it was Bertha.
canonical_facts.supernatural_call: Chapter 35. Jane hears Rochester's voice calling 'Jane! Jane! Jane!' across the moors as she is about to yield to St John. Rochester later confirms (Ch 37) he cried out her name in prayer at that moment.
canonical_facts.ferndean: Small, secluded manor in woods owned by Rochester. He retreats there after the fire. Jane reunites with him in Chapter 37.

issues.claim: Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the male pen name Currer Bell.
issues.correct: 'Currer Bell' was a gender-ambiguous name, not explicitly male. The Brontë sisters chose names (Currer, Ellis, Acton) that could be read either way to avoid gender prejudice. 'Male pen name' is a common GCSE simplification and is not significantly misleading, but 'gender-ambiguous pen name' is more accurate.

issues.claim: The dfn tooltip defines typhus as 'An infectious disease, often called consumption, that was a major killer in Victorian Britain, especially among the poor and malnourished.'
issues.correct: Typhus and consumption (tuberculosis) are completely different diseases. Typhus is a louse/flea-borne bacterial infection (Rickettsia). Consumption is tuberculosis, a mycobacterial infection. Calling typhus 'often called consumption' is factually wrong and will actively mislead students.

issues.claim: a typhus epidemic sweeps through the school, killing many students — including Jane's closest friend, Helen Burns
issues.correct: The typhus epidemic does sweep Lowood and kills many students, but Helen Burns does NOT die of typhus. Helen dies of consumption (tuberculosis), a separate pre-existing condition, in Chapter 9. Jane slips to Miss Temple's room to be with Helen and wakes to find she has died with Jane's arms around her neck. This is one of the most commonly tested facts about the novel.

issues.location: Lowood section, same paragraph — conflated context
issues.claim: Brontë based these scenes on her own experience at the Clergy Daughters' School, where her sisters Maria and Elizabeth contracted tuberculosis and died. [This immediately follows the claim that Helen died of typhus]
issues.correct: The proximity creates an internally contradictory passage: Helen dies of 'typhus' but the sisters died of 'tuberculosis'. Brontë's sisters dying of TB directly inspired Helen Burns dying of consumption (TB). The juxtaposition reinforces rather than corrects the disease confusion in the preceding sentence.

issues.location: Key quotations bank, Gender & Independence section
issues.claim: 'A curious laugh — distinct, formal, mirthless.' (Ch. 11) — the Gothic description of Bertha's laughter
issues.correct: The quote is accurate. Jane first hears the laugh in Ch. 11 when she arrives at Thornfield. Chapter attribution is approximately correct (some editions have the first mention in Ch. 11 or 12 depending on pagination). No significant error.

issues.location: Paragraph on Adèle and Brontë's use of character
issues.claim: Adèle is lively but superficial, obsessed with gifts and dresses (Brontë uses her to gently satirise French vanity)
issues.correct: The characterisation is broadly accurate — Adèle is associated with gifts, performance, and dressing up. 'French vanity' as the satirical target is a narrow reading; Brontë uses Adèle more to contrast with Jane's depth of character and to explore Rochester's sense of obligation. Not a factual error — interpretive framing.

issues.claim: 'the clothed hyena' who runs at Rochester with 'something of vengeance'
issues.correct: Minor paraphrase: In the novel (Ch 26) 'the clothed hyena rose up, and stood tall on its hind-feet' — the hyena image describes Bertha rising/standing, not specifically running at Rochester. 'Something of vengeance' is accurate and appears in the same chapter. The combination is a slight paraphrase but not a significant error.

issues.claim: He survived, but was left blinded and with one hand amputated.
issues.correct: Accurate but imprecise: the novel specifies it is Rochester's LEFT hand that was crushed and amputated by the surgeon Mr Carter. Adding 'left' would improve precision for students writing about the symbolism of the injury.

issues.claim: Helen dies of consumption after a typhus epidemic sweeps the school
issues.correct: Internally contradictory. If Helen dies of consumption, the typhus epidemic is not what killed her. The typhus epidemic kills other Lowood students; Helen Burns dies separately of her pre-existing tuberculosis (consumption) in Chapter 9. The sentence should separate the two events clearly: the typhus epidemic kills many students; Helen, separately, is dying of consumption.

issues.location: Lowood section, description of Cowan Bridge
issues.claim: Lowood School is modelled on Cowan Bridge, the charity school that killed two of Brontë's own sisters
issues.correct: The school's harsh conditions contributed to the deaths of Maria and Elizabeth Brontë, but they were removed from the school and died at home in Haworth (Maria 6 May 1825, Elizabeth 15 June 1825). The school did not 'kill' them in the direct sense; they died of tuberculosis whose progression was hastened by Cowan Bridge's poor conditions.

issues.location: The Interruption at the Altar section
issues.claim: Briggs announces: 'I affirm and can prove that Edward Fairfax Rochester was, on the 20th of October... married to my sister, Bertha Antoinetta Mason'
issues.correct: Minor attribution confusion: in the novel, Mr Briggs presents the legal written evidence (as John Eyre's solicitor), but 'my sister' is Richard Mason's language, not Briggs's. Briggs and Mason both speak at the interrupted wedding — the lesson conflates their separate testimonies into one speech attributed to Briggs. The substance (bigamous marriage confirmed) is accurate.

issues.location: The Wedding and the Revelation section
issues.claim: His wife, Bertha Mason, is alive and imprisoned in the attic at Thornfield.
issues.correct: The novel consistently places Bertha in the 'third floor' or 'third storey' of Thornfield, not technically an attic. This is a widespread simplification across teaching materials and not seriously misleading at GCSE level, but the novel's language is 'third storey'.

issues.claim: Rochester survived but was blinded and lost a hand trying to save the servants and Bertha.
issues.correct: Accurate but could specify: Rochester's LEFT hand was crushed and amputated. Rochester regains partial sight in ONE eye (not full vision) two years after marriage.

issues.claim: Rochester calls her 'my Indian Messalina' — a reference to a notoriously dissolute Roman empress, combined with a colonial label that links her madness to her Creole origins.
issues.correct: The quote 'my Indian Messalina' is accurate and from Chapter 27, so there is no factual error in the quotation itself. However, the lesson presents it as a descriptor of who Bertha is rather than framing it as Rochester's self-serving, prejudiced characterisation. For exam purposes, students should be taught to treat this as Rochester's biased voice, not Brontë's authorial description. The phrase reflects Rochester's racial and colonial attitudes. Minor framing issue, not a factual error per se.

issues.location: Quotation bank at end of lesson
issues.claim: 'I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun' (Rochester's growth). Learn them all.
issues.correct: This quote does NOT appear in Jane Eyre. It is spoken by Mr Darcy in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, Chapter 60, when he explains to Elizabeth how he fell in love with her. Students who memorise this as a Jane Eyre quotation and use it in a Jane Eyre exam answer would be penalised. The quotation must be removed from this lesson.

critical_findings: AQA L2 (2fe05d71): TWO high-severity errors in the same lesson. (1) dfn tooltip defines typhus as 'often called consumption' — factually wrong, they are completely different diseases. (2) States Helen Burns was killed by the typhus epidemic — Helen dies of consumption (TB) in Ch 9, a separate cause of death from the typhus that kills other students. This lesson requires two fixes and is the most error-dense in the set.

Eduqas L8 (bfd272f4): Quotes 'I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun' as a Jane Eyre quotation about Rochester's growth. This is Mr Darcy's line from Pride and Prejudice Ch 60 — it does not exist in Jane Eyre. Students using it in an exam would be penalised.

OCR L2 (ec99594f): Two medium issues. (1) Helen dies 'of consumption after a typhus epidemic' — internally contradictory phrasing that links her death to the typhus when she dies of consumption. (2) Cowan Bridge described as the school that 'killed' Brontë's sisters — inaccurate; the sisters were removed and died at home.
summary.cross_board_pattern: The Helen Burns cause-of-death confusion is the dominant pattern across boards: AQA L2 is outright wrong (typhus killed Helen), OCR L2 is contradictory ('consumption after typhus'). Edexcel L2 and Eduqas L2 handle the distinction correctly. The 'attic' vs 'third floor/storey' simplification appears in multiple lessons across all boards but is low-severity.
summary.clean_lessons_note: 17 of 31 lessons have no issues. All Reunion/Resolution and most Thornfield/Rochester lessons are factually clean. All Context lessons except AQA L1 (pen-name framing, low) are clean.
